record.original_question: Does every connected d-regular graph G admit a signature σ whose signed adjacency matrix has spectral radius at most 2 sqrt(d - 1)?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 3.20 (Bilu-Linial [8]). Every connected d-regular graph G has a signature σ with spectral radius at most 2 √ d − 1.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected $d$-regular graph on $n$ vertices, with $d\ge 2$. A signature of $G$ is a function $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$. The signed adjacency matrix $A_\sigma$ is the $n\times n$ symmetric matrix whose $(u,v)$-entry equals $\sigma(\{u,v\})$ if $\{u,v\}\in E$ and $0$ otherwise. Its spectral radius is $\rho(A_\sigma)=\max_i |\lambda_i(A_\sigma)|$.

Prove or disprove: for every connected $d$-regular graph $G$, there exists a signature $\sigma:E\to\{+1,-1\}$ such that
$$\rho(A_\sigma)\;\le\; 2\sqrt{d-1}.$$
artifact.status_search_result: The Bilu–Linial conjecture is still open in full generality. Bilu and Linial (2006) proved a weaker bound of order $\sqrt{d\log^3 d}$. Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava (2015) established the bipartite case via interlacing families, yielding bipartite Ramanujan graphs of every degree, but the non-bipartite case remains unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Interlacing families I: Bipartite Ramanujan graphs of all degrees
status_evidence.snippet: Proves the Bilu–Linial conjecture for bipartite graphs by analyzing expected characteristic polynomials of randomly signed adjacency matrices.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is proved for bipartite d-regular graphs.

status_evidence.title: Signing a graph to have small magnitude eigenvalues — Open Problem Garden
status_evidence.snippet: Lists the Bilu–Linial conjecture as an open problem on signing graphs to obtain spectral radius at most 2√(d−1).
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture remains listed as open in general.

status_evidence.title: Unsolved Problems in Spectral Graph Theory
status_evidence.snippet: Survey discusses Bilu–Linial as still open beyond the bipartite case.
status_evidence.claim: Recent surveys treat the conjecture as open in the non-bipartite case.
